title: Whale falls: deep-sea communities on sunken whale carcasses and the bone-eating Osedax worms

sources.title: Ever since there have been whales, there have been Osedax worms eating their bones

facts.text: During a 2019 expedition, researchers found a whale fall 10,623 feet (about 3,200 meters) below the surface near Davidson Seamount in NOAA’s Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, off central California.
The 2019 discovery was made with a remotely operated vehicle from the research ship E/V Nautilus and was streamed live; eelpouts, octopuses and worms were seen feeding on the skeleton.
The deep sea is cold, dark and under immense pressure, and most animals there live on marine snow: dead plankton, waste and other material drifting down from the surface.

Craig Smith and Amanda Demopoulos estimated that a decomposing 40-ton whale carcass can supply about 50 square meters of sea floor with as much carbon as normal marine snow brings in about 2,000 years.
Whale-fall ecosystems were first studied in 1988 by a University of Hawaii team led by Craig Smith.
First stage of a whale fall: mobile scavengers such as sharks, hagfish and rattails eat the soft tissue in a matter of months.
Second stage (enrichment-opportunist): smaller animals such as little worms and crustaceans live in the sediment around the bones, which is enriched with scraps of tissue for over a year.

Third stage, by far the longest: bacteria break down fat in the bones and produce hydrogen sulfide, which other bacteria use for energy; mats of bacteria and animals such as clams can live on a skeleton for years to decades.
Scientists suspect a fourth, reef stage, in which animals that filter food from the water settle on the bare bones.

Osedax worms were first found in 2002 by researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, who came across a whale skeleton covered with worms while searching for clam beds in Monterey Canyon, about 3,000 meters deep.
Osedax is Latin for bone devourer. Female Osedax worms have no eyes, mouth or stomach; they grow green roots into whale bone, and bacteria living inside the roots digest the fats.
Osedax worms release acid through their roots to dissolve the hard bone material.
Male Osedax worms are microscopic, and a female can hold up to 100 males.
Fossil whale bones about 30 million years old show holes made by Osedax worms, suggesting the worms have fed on whales for as long as there have been whales.

notes: 具體事件用 2019 年 E/V Nautilus 在蒙特雷灣國家海洋保護區拍到的鯨落（NOAA、NPR）與 2002 年在蒙特雷峽谷發現的食骨蠕蟲（Nature 新聞、National Geographic）。10,623 英尺換算約 3,238 公尺，文中寫 more than 3,200 meters。
